metadata.title: RICE-HUSK BIOCHAR AND TRICHODERMA FORTIFICATION MODULATE THE CHEMICAL AND MICROBIOLOGICAL PROFILES OF  ORGANIC-WASTE LIQUID FERTILIZER
metadata.description: Liquid organic fertilizer (LOF) derived from mixed organic residues may promote nutrient circularity; however, its chemical quality and microbial viability depend on formulation and fermentation conditions. This study assessed the effects of rice-husk biochar and Trichoderma spp. fortification on LOF produced from banana peel, pineapple peel, rabbit urine, and molasses in a passively aerated stacked-bucket system. A randomized complete block design included four treatments with four replicates: unfortified LOF (P1), Trichoderma alone (P2), 1% w/v biochar (P3), and biochar plus Trichoderma (P4). Chemical variables were analyzed by ANOVA followed by Tukey's HSD test at 5%, whereas microbial and metal data were interpreted descriptively. Fortification did not affect pH (7.20–7.22). P3 had the highest organic C (0.58%) and C/N ratio (5.92), whereas P4 had the highest total N (0.12%), P (0.22%), and K (0.62%). P2 had the highest total fungal count (7.2 × 10⁵ CFU mL⁻¹) and recoverable Trichoderma population (6.5 × 10⁵ CFU mL⁻¹); corresponding values in P4 were 3.8 × 10⁵ and 3.5 × 10⁵ CFU mL⁻¹. Co-fortification improved macronutrient profiles but did not maximize Trichoderma recovery from the liquid fraction. Further optimization and plant-based efficacy testing are required.

metadata.title: The network that learned to run itself
metadata.description: The limitations of traditional automation with scale and complexity have given rise to a powerful new concept - hyper-automation - Mostly for IT and cybersecurity areas. It is a system that allows machines to be self-managed and self-adaptive through AI, machine learning, and software orchestration, reducing human intervention. Streaming services, IoT sensors, and remote works are just some of the main drivers that bring about the need to shift traditional rule-based automation to proactive, self-regulating networks, which are enabled by real-time monitoring and decision-making like, for example, congestion prevention and resource allocation done autonomously by AIOps tools. So, 24x7 security, with minimum downtime and human error, is possible to achieve by organizations. Meanwhile, the reliance on autonomous systems creates important questions about trust responsibility accountability and Because of this, the necessity of effective oversight as well as the presence of highly trained personnel who are capable of handling these technologies will become paramount to the equation. Businesses that implement hyper-automation [1] well may end up far ahead of the competitors that still rely on manual processes. It just goes to show that as the network landscape evolves, the organizations that are going to thrive are the ones adopting hyper-automation at a deep level. In the end, getting on board with hyper-automation is not only a futuristic consideration, it is a requirement for organizations who desire to be competitive in the digital world.[14][15][16][17]

metadata.title: IAUC Systematic Literature Review: Extraction Protocol, Metadata, and Validation Data
metadata.description:
Data and code archive for a systematic review of the urban climate literature, in which large language models extracted structured metadata from the full text of every paper in the corpus.

Contents

  • data/extracted_metadata/ — 9,284 canonical per-paper JSON records
  • data/enrichments/ and data/contribution_rationales/ — 9,284 per-paper enrichment and rationale records
  • data/volunteer_review/ — anonymised expert validation responses
  • data/cross_model_validation/ — model comparisons supporting the extraction choice, plus later isolated noncanonical GPT-5.6 audits that do not replace the canonical corpus or feed manuscript results
  • src/, tests/, Makefile, and uv.lock — the analysis pipeline and paper-reproducibility test suite

Reproducing the analysis

uv sync --extra dev then make paper-all rebuilds the consolidated corpus and manuscript statistics. make ci-test runs the offline tests shipped with the package.

Licensing

Everything in this deposit — data and code alike — is released under CC-BY-4.0.

This version

Refreshes the revised-manuscript archive after the final plotting audit and adds portable records from subsequent, explicitly noncanonical extraction comparisons. Canonical Gemini records, corpus membership, and manuscript results are unchanged.

metadata.title: Dominant Regulatory Axis Detection (DRA)
metadata.description:
Dominant Regulatory Axis Detection (DRA): A Mechanistic, Low‑Dimensional Approach for Identifying Major Transcriptional Shifts in Clinical RNA‑seq and Single‑Cell Studies

Abstract

Dominant Regulatory Axis (DRA) is a lightweight, mechanistically grounded method for identifying the strongest transcriptional regulatory shift between two biological or clinical states. Instead of producing long, diffuse pathway lists, DRA isolates the top magnitude‑of‑change genes and maps them to compact transcription factor signatures, yielding interpretable axis scores such as NFκB, p53, or NR3C1. The method is robust to cohort heterogeneity, simple to deploy, and suitable for clinical‑trial pipelines. This deposit includes a reference implementation, minimal TF signatures, example data, documentation, provenance, and an optional integration provision for GeneXplain.

Description

Background

Relapse biology in acute myeloid leukemia and other clinical contexts often converges on a small number of dominant transcriptional axes rather than broad, evenly distributed pathway changes. DRA operationalizes this observation by ranking genes by magnitude of change between two states and mapping the strongest changes to curated TF signatures. The result is a single dominant regulatory axis per sample, providing mechanistic clarity without computational overhead.

Method Overview

  • Input: bulk or single‑cell RNA‑seq expression matrices and metadata defining two states.

  • Gene ranking: median‑based log2 fold change or other robust delta metrics.

  • Max‑delta selection: top N genes by absolute change (default N = 300).

  • Signature mapping: intersection with minimal TF signatures.

  • Axis scoring: per‑gene z‑scoring followed by mean signature expression.

  • Output: axis scores and dominant axis labels per sample.

Key Advantages

  • Mechanistic interpretability through TF axis activation.

  • Robustness to cohort heterogeneity.

  • Simplicity of deployment and reproducibility.

  • Extensibility to custom signatures or alternative scoring methods.

Practical Course‑of‑Action Guide

This deposit includes a practical guide designed to help users navigate Windows, PowerShell, and Python environments without relying on rigid step‑by‑step instructions. The guide outlines the sequence of decisions and actions needed to run DRA reliably:

  1. Establish a working directory.

  2. Confirm Python availability.

  3. Create a clean environment (venv or conda).

  4. Verify file paths and permissions.

  5. Run the pipeline on example data.

  6. Interpret axis scores and dominant axis labels.

  7. Scale up to real datasets.

  8. Optionally integrate with GeneXplain.

  9. Troubleshoot systematically.

  10. Maintain reproducibility practices.

This approach is resilient to differences in system configuration and avoids the pitfalls of overly rigid workflows.

Methods Summary

Core Algorithm

  • Compute per‑gene delta between states using median‑based log2 fold change.

  • Select top N genes by absolute delta.

  • Map selected genes to TF signatures.

  • Z‑score selected genes across samples.

  • Compute axis scores as mean z‑scores across signature genes.

  • Assign dominant axis per sample.

Parameter Guidance

  • topN: default 300; adjust for cohort size.

  • Delta metric: log2 fold change or robust alternatives.

  • Scoring: mean z‑score or more advanced methods (GSEA, regulon activity).

Implementation Notes

  • Uses an appropriate Python version with standard scientific libraries.

  • Containerization recommended for exact reproducibility.

  • Signature curation is intentionally minimal and transparent.

Provenance and Reproducibility

The deposit includes a populated PROVENANCE.txt documenting:

  • Version: 1.0.0

  • Date: 2026‑07‑04

  • Contact email: v_spiros@hotmail.com

  • Software environment described in general terms

  • Processing steps

  • Default parameters

  • Output descriptions

  • Checksums

  • Licensing

  • GeneXplain integration notes

  • Changelog

Reproducibility recommendations include recording environment details, using containerization, and validating signature overlap.

Files Included

This deposit uses a simplified three‑mother‑file structure:

Mother File

Contents

dra_package_code_signatures

Code, signatures, examples, requirements

dra_documentation_bundle

README, methods, one‑page summary, provenance, integration provision

metadata_and_related_1_1

Related identifiers and metadata manifest

This structure minimizes upload complexity while preserving clarity and completeness.

GeneXplain Integration (Optional)

DRA outputs (axis_scores.tsv, dominant_axis.tsv, and top_genes/) are formatted for optional import into GeneXplain for enrichment and causal network analysis. This integration is optional, not required. Proprietary GeneXplain project files are not included.

Version

1.1.1

Portions of the documentation and metadata were prepared with assistance from Microsoft Copilot. All scientific content, code, and decisions were made by the author.

Version v4 update: This version adds the TE‑chromVAR module, including background model construction, deviation scoring, TE‑stemness computation, and watcher integration. Documentation and changelog are included in the files TE_Chromvar_and_related_README.md and TE_Changelog.txt.

Version v5 update: In connection to the TE‑chromVAR module enabling transposable‑element–centric regulatory axis detection across scATAC‑seq datasets:

Added new AML stemness reference: Transposable elements shape stemness in normal and leukemic hematopoiesis (Grillo et al., Nat Genet 2026), expanding the conceptual foundation for TE‑driven regulatory modeling.

Updated documentation to clarify the role of TE subfamilies (ERV1/ERV3/LTR12C) in AML stemness and their integration into DRA’s mechanistic framework.

Version v6 update: Adds runnable example (dra_code/), demonstration figure, and TE‑chromVAR integration for reproducibility. This version completes the DRA framework with a runnable example and visual demonstration. A new folder dra_code/ has been added, containing dra_run.py and a minimal synthetic dataset (example_data/adata_example.h5ad, te_peaks_example.csv) that allows users to execute the pipeline end‑to‑end. A conceptual UMAP schematic illustrates TE‑stemness distribution and clarifies interpretation of the TE‑chromVAR integration. All prior modules (chromvar_background.py, deviation.py, stemness.py, watcher_hooks.py) remain unchanged. This update makes the record fully reproducible and visually self‑contained for teaching and demonstration purposes.

metadata.title: Promoting inclusive rural development: A mixed-methods evaluation of TEKAD's impact in eastern Indonesia
metadata.description:
Persistent rural disparities in Indonesia’s eastern provinces necessitate innovative, inclusive development approaches.

The Transformasi Ekonomi Kampung Terpadu (TEKAD) program, a partnership between the Indonesian

government and the International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD), aims to transform rural

economies through participatory planning, micro-enterprise support, and enhanced financial and institutional

access. This study employs a sequential mixed-methods approach, analysing quantitative data from 698

households across 47 villages in ten regencies at Eastern Indonesia namely, Papua Island, Nusa Tenggara Timur

and Maluku, complemented by qualitative insights from interviews and observations. This research found that

the program’s outcomes exceed the targets for financial access and market access but underperformed in productivity,

technology adoption, institutional trust, and investment satisfaction, particularly in fisheries and regions

with weak governance. People with disabilities faced significant exclusion, highlighting deficiencies in

TEKAD’s Gender Equality, Disability, and Social Inclusion (GEDSI) framework. The study reveals tensions between

decentralized development and implementation consistency, aligning with adaptive governance scholarship.

Recommendations include context-sensitive strategies, universal design principles, and integrated value-

chain planning to enhance equitable rural transformation in Indonesia and similar settings.

metadata.title: Association between Personality Traits, Work-Family Conflict, Job Stress and Nurses' Cognitive Failures: A Cross-Sectional Study
metadata.description: Background: Cognitive failures are one of the most important causes of patients' unsafe events. Hence, it is necessary to consider individual and cognitive, as well as extra-organizational characteristics. The present study was conducted to investigate the association between personality traits, job stress, work-family conflict and nurses' cognitive failures. Materials and Methods: This descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted among 250 nurses working in three public hospitals in Sari city, Iran, in 2021. The subjects were selected using Stratified Random Sampling. NEO Five-Factor Inventory, Health and Safety Executive (HSE) tool, Work-Family Conflict Scale (WFCS), and Occupational Cognitive Failure Questionnaire (OCFQ) were used to measure personality traits, job stress, work-family conflict, and cognitive Failures, respectively. The data were analyzed in SPSS (ve. 23) and regression analysis with the sequential method was applied. Results: Among 13 studied predictor variables, only extraversion, agreeableness, demand, and role were predictors of cognitive failures. These variables explain 44.1% of the variance of cognitive failure. The Β values of neuroticism and conscientiousness to predict cognitive failures were 0.34 and -0.29, respectively (P < 0.001). Although role (Β = 0.15, p < 0.001) and demand (Β = 0.14, p < 0.001) significantly predict cognitive failure; however, their effect is limited. The results of the study did not provide confirmation for the moderating effect of neuroticism, extraversion, agreeableness, and conscientiousness on the association between work-family conflict, job stress, and cognitive failures. Conclusions: Along with environmental and organizational stress factors, evaluating nurses’ personality traits is necessary to control cognitive failures.

metadata.title: POLICY-DRIVEN REVITALISATION OF SOUTH AFRICAN MINING TOWNS: FROM EXTRACTION TO SUSTAINABLE COMMUNITIES
metadata.description: Abstract: Mining has been central to South Africa's economic development for over a century, contributing significantly to national income, employment, exports and industrialisation. However, despite their substantial economic contribution, many mining towns continue to experience persistent socio-economic challenges, including unemployment, poverty, deteriorating infrastructure, environmental degradation, weak municipal governance and limited economic diversification. This study examines the effectiveness of South Africa's policy and governance framework in revitalising mining towns into sustainable, resilient and inclusive communities. It seeks to develop a comprehensive policy-driven framework that promotes long-term socio-economic development, environmental sustainability and post-mining community resilience. The development of South African mining towns has largely been driven by extractive economic activities rather than sustainable territorial development. Although the country has established an extensive legislative and policy framework—including the Mineral and Petroleum Resources Development Act, the Mining Charter, Social and Labour Plans, the National Development Plan 2030, the District Development Model and the Spatial Planning and Land Use Management Act—implementation remains fragmented, poorly coordinated and inconsistently monitored. Consequently, many mining communities continue to experience governance failures, inadequate service delivery, declining municipal capacity and economic vulnerability, particularly in the context of mine closures and the Just Energy Transition. The absence of an integrated policy framework for sustainable mining-town revitalisation represents a significant gap in both policy and scholarly literature. The study adopts a qualitative research approach based on an extensive review and critical analysis of secondary data. Data were obtained from peer-reviewed journal articles, government legislation, policy documents, official reports, municipal governance reports, international development publications and industry reports relating to mining-town development in South Africa. A thematic content analysis was employed to identify recurring governance, policy, socio-economic and environmental issues affecting mining communities. The analysis further examined the alignment and effectiveness of existing legislative and institutional frameworks in promoting sustainable local development and identified international best practices relevant to the South African context. The study finds that South Africa possesses a comprehensive legislative and policy framework to support sustainable mining-community development; however, implementation is constrained by fragmented governance, weak intergovernmental coordination, limited municipal capacity, inadequate monitoring of Social and Labour Plans and insufficient community participation. The findings further reveal that many mining towns remain economically dependent on mineral extraction, making them vulnerable to mine closures, commodity market fluctuations and the transition towards a low-carbon economy. Environmental degradation, deteriorating infrastructure and limited economic diversification continue to undermine long-term community resilience. The study concludes that sustainable revitalisation requires integrated governance, stronger institutional collaboration, effective policy implementation, economic diversification, environmental rehabilitation, inclusive stakeholder participation and improved municipal planning. The study concludes that the future sustainability of South Africa's mining towns depends on a deliberate transition from extraction-driven development towards integrated, policy-driven community revitalisation. Sustainable mining communities cannot be achieved through isolated corporate social investment initiatives or fragmented government interventions alone. Instead, coordinated governance.
keywords: Mining towns; Sustainable communities; Policy-driven revitalisation; Sustainable development; Mineral and Petroleum Resources Development Act (MPRDA); Local economic development; Municipal governance; Economic diversification; Social and Labour Plans (SLPs); Environmental rehabilitation; Mining policy; Community resilience; Public policy; Integrated development planning; Just Energy Transition; Infrastructure development; Resource governance; Post-mining development; South Africa; Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

metadata.title: PGSD Eccentricity Demonstration Reproducibility Package v1.1
metadata.description:
Version 1.1 - corrected reference-sphere geometry

This repository provides the data, analysis code, numerical outputs, and documentation required to reproduce the center-eccentricity demonstration presented in the manuscript:

“Physics-Guided Scientific Discovery (PGSD): A Reference Architecture for Explainable Knowledge Generation in Mechanical Engineering.”

Version 1.1 supersedes version 1.0. It corrects the reference-sphere diameter from 24.9984 mm to 24.98484 mm and consequently updates the effective probe-center contact radius to:

R_e = 15.49242 mm.

The original CNC measurement files are preserved unchanged. The correction affects the contact-geometry constants, the constant-radius interpretation, and the calculated higher-order contact scale. It does not change the first-order LFH differential coefficient pair because those coefficients are estimated from the measured-coordinate columns and angular directions.

The demonstration uses two CNC touch-probing acquisitions of the reference sphere, denoted X0Y0 and LT_X0Y0, each containing 32 equatorial measurement points. A nominal relative offset of (-0.300, -0.300) mm was introduced through the CNC/G54 command between the two acquisitions.

The package includes:

  • the original CNC measurement files in CMM format;
  • normalized coordinate datasets;
  • Python scripts for Local Fourier Harmonic analysis and circle fitting;
  • numerical results corresponding to the manuscript;
  • files used to reproduce Figure 4;
  • documentation of the coordinate convention, units, sampling sequence, contact-geometry constants, and execution procedure;
  • a version history and correction note;
  • a package manifest and SHA-256 checksums.

The package reproduces the first-order LFH differential coefficient pair:

  • Delta a1 = -0.299865 mm
  • Delta b1 = -0.300743 mm

and the corresponding provisional inferred magnitude of 0.424695 mm. Using the corrected effective contact radius, the characteristic second-order contact scale is 2.90465 micrometres.

The nominal CNC/G54-commanded offset was not independently measured using an external calibrated displacement reference. Therefore, the numerical differences between the LFH estimate and the nominal command must not be interpreted as independently verified displacement errors. Only one acquisition was available for each state, and no complete uncertainty budget, within-state repeatability study, or multi-state validation was performed. The reported coefficient pair is consequently classified as a physically and operationally corroborated Candidate Signature, not as a validated or canonical Signature.

Changes from version 1.0

  • corrected the reference-sphere diameter to 24.98484 mm;
  • updated the effective contact radius to 15.49242 mm;
  • updated the higher-order contact-scale calculation to 2.90465 micrometres;
  • updated the analysis documentation, numerical metadata, and checksums;
  • preserved the original CMM measurement files;
  • confirmed that the first-order LFH differential coefficients and provisional inverse estimate remain unchanged.

This package supports Section 6 of the PGSD Foundation Preprint v1.2.
